MR. ALEXANDER-INCORRECT ATTRIBUTION BY "GLOBE AND MAIL" OF CERTAIN STATEMENTS TO MINISTER OF MANPOWER AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I think will be of interest to all members of the House. I am sure that after I have related the facts Your Honour will find in my favour.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) made a statement on November 7 dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Act and it was duly reported in the Globe and Mail on Thursday, November 8. One never likes to question the Globe and Mail, but apparently statements which should have been attributed to me have been attributed to the minister.
I suggest that the statements are of some significance and I would not want to embarrass the minister. In the article, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is reported to have said:
I should like to say that one of the most disastrous things we have done in this House is to remove the $800-million statutory ceiling because this means that the members of the opposition and the people of Canada can never tell in what state the Unemployment Insurance Fund is at any particular time unless the minister stands up and makes a statement.
But that is not all. I questioned the disincentive aspects of the bill. In that regard the statement is reported to have been made by the minister:
This is a question which has been asked by employers across this country who advise that the disincentive aspects of the bill, in fact, are eroding the free enterprise system.
There is a further statement of some consequence that I think would be embarrassing to the minister. I indicated that because of government mismanagement the minister 0 had found it necessary to increase the employee contribution to $1.40. The following statement is also attributed to the minister:
This is an unwarranted tax because of government mismanagement.
Finally, there is this last and most important statement. I reviewed the entire matter and, keeping in mind the lack of significant projections as to the cost of the scheme and the amount of the benefits, I concluded with this statement which is also attributed to the minister:
In every instance the government is wrong and that is why I say this bill which, in the first instance the members of this House thought would be a good bill, is a fraud of some significant proportions upon the House of Commons and the people of Canada.
I think this is a matter of some significance. I know I speak on behalf of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration when I say that this is certainly a question of privilege. Through Your Honour's good offices, perhaps the Globe and Mail could be instructed to make another run at the matter in order to show the true facts. I am sure the minister may have some misgivings about the work of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, but I do not think he has the gall or the nerve to stand up and make the statements I did.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ALEXANDER-INCORRECT ATTRIBUTION BY "GLOBE AND MAIL" OF CERTAIN STATEMENTS TO MINISTER OF MANPOWER AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Order, please. The minister will, of course, be recognized, even though I am not sure whether the hon. member's question of privilege is raised with tongue in cheek. Whether it is or not, I remind hon. members there is a requirement that notice ought to be given to the Chair. It seems to me hon. members have a tendency to disregard the provisions of the Standing Order which insist that notice ought to be given in advance of questions of privilege or of motions under Standing Order 26. I would hope all hon. members will keep that in mind. It is helpful to the Chair. Having said that, I appreciate the way the matter was brought before the House by the hon. member and I have no hesitation in allowing the minister to comment.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind hon. members that the day after tomorrow is Remembrance Day. It will mark the fifty-fifth anniversary of the ceasefire in the first world war.
It is the day our country officially observes as the day of remembrance for those Canadian men and women who gave their lives in the defence of freedom. In two world wars and the Korean campaign nearly 115,000 Canadians
7692

November 9, 1973
Remembrance Day
made the supreme sacrifice. This Sunday, at 11 a.m., that sacrifice will be remembered not only in Ottawa but all across Canada and in many other parts of the world. Our allies also keep November 11a sacred day to pay tribute to those who laid down their lives so that we and our children can live a serene and rewarding life.
There are many vacant chairs in Canadian homes today which belonged to fathers, husbands and sons who never came home from the wars. There are also many chairs which are filled by those who bear physical evidence of the scars and wounds of battle. These, also, we remember. Not just on November 11, but all through the year. The memorials we have erected to the fallen, both at home and abroad, pay dignified and worthy tribute to those whose names they commemorate. We are proud of them just as we are proud of the ways in which the people of this country have always acknowledged the debt which is owed to those who survived.
I feel that Canada, in her remembrance of both the living and the dead, has respected and honoured those who served in as fine a way as any country in the world. I feel we have caught the torch which was thrown to us in the immortal words of John McCrae. Let us for ever hold it high.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party I am happy to endorse the statement just made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. As a matter of fact, as Your Honour will recall, I spoke to you this morning to indicate that I intended to rise to make a motion on this subject. I therefore heartily endorse the minister's statement.
I hope the ceremonies on the fifty-fifth anniversary of the ending of the first world war will remind the government that there are still some inequities in the veterans legislation. I know that the 52 members of the House of Commons who are war veterans realize this and will dedicate themselves to fulfilling the obligations that successive prime ministers have undertaken to the veterans of Canada.
I might take this opportunity to call the attention of the House to the fact that we still have among us a member of the House of Commons who is also a veteran of the first world war in the person of the distinguished right hon. member for Prince Albert.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate the New Democratic Party with the remarks made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs concerning Remembrance Day. Those who will march in the parades to be held across Canada on November 11 will be remembering intimately their comrades who died in the service of their country, those who suffered in that service, all those who took part in wars which they and the country believed were necessary for the survival of our democratic system and our nation.
There are many young people today who will watch these parades with some interest and little knowledge. I hope that Remembrance Day will direct the attention of

those Canadians who have no knowledge of the wars to the efforts that Canada can well make by playing an independent role in the world and trying to fulfil the obligations that those who fought and died for Canada in two great wars were trying to accomplish. We can do this effectively and efficiently by remaining independent and maintaining a peacekeeping role throughout the world, thus eliminating the suffering, loss and grief caused those who gave so much in two world wars and in Korea.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE BY MINISTER OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like our colleagues in this House, we are very happy to join the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) and all the people of Canada in paying tribute next Monday to those who died for their country.
If Canada still enjoys the total freedom that many other countries do not have, perhaps we owe it to those who are no longer among us or who gave their health and their limbs in the two previous world wars.
In the name of my colleagues and the Canadian population, I should like to thank those who gave us yesterday the freedom which we enjoy today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON DEPLOYMENT OF CANADIAN LOGISTICS
subsubtopic: CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1 I informed the House that it was my intention to meet with the Secretary General of the United Nations in New York the following day to discuss with him the composition of the emergency force for service in the Middle East. My discussions with the Secretary General were useful and served to clarify some of the outstanding issues.
The same evening agreement was reached in the Security Council authorizing the Secretary General to consult with potential contributors, including Canada and Poland who were to provide contingents which would have particular responsibility for the provision of logistic support. On November 5 following my return from the United Nations I tabled in the House the text of the Security Council agreement along with the texts of notes exchanged between the Secretary General and our ambassador to the United Nations.	f
Our ambassador has since been holding discussions with the Secretary General, at Mr. Waldheim's request, concerning the organization and composition of the logistics element of the United Nations Emergency Force. Polish representatives have also participated in these more detailed discussions. Meanwhile, evaluation teams were dispatched to Cairo to assess the requirement on the ground.
In the light of the discussions to date, I wish to inform the House that agreement has been reached on the first phase of the deployment of the Canadian contingent. A signals unit which will provide communications for the United Nations Emergency Force will begin its departure
November 9, 1973

from Canada within the next few days. We understand the Poles will be dispatching an engineer unit as the first element in their contribution. In the meantime, the Secretary General is awaiting the final reports of the evaluation teams and continuing his discussions with Canadian and Polish representatives to determine the next stages of the logistics deployment. These discussions have, of course, even greater urgency than heretofore in light of the news that progress has been made in securing a truce and in initiating negotiations which we all hope will lead to a permanent settlement.
As Canada will shortly be dispatching a signals unit to the Middle East, I propose to bring forward in the House on Tuesday, November 13, the resolution seeking the approval of parliament for the government's decision to participate in the UNEF.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON DEPLOYMENT OF CANADIAN LOGISTICS
subsubtopic: CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the minister indicates that the government is preparing to go ahead with a contingent for the peace force in the Middle East. We say bon voyage and best wishes to the signals upit about to leave Canada within the next few days.
The encouraging developments this week in the Middle East make it difficult for any responsible observer to suggest any posture on our part that could in any way add an extra dimension of difficulty to the situation. However, there remain some fundamental questions as to why our government pursued participation so vehemently and why the minister felt it necessary to ensure that Canada was part of the peace force. Surely our nation's foreign policies are not so fragile as to require the biannual injections of peace force participation in order to stay healthy.
My colleagues and I will have more specific matters to raise with reference not only to our participation in the Middle East peacekeeping force but on the entire question of peace force use and our role within peace forces when the resolution is brought forward for debate on Tuesday. That Canada should respond to international requests for assistance is beyond question; that Canada should insist on participating in every international peace force is truly open to question.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that next Tuesday's debate will be a real one and not only a series of monologues like in the past.
If the minister really wants the agreement of this House, I hope he will give us all the necessary data and inform us of the position of the government and of its policy as regards a peacekeeping force. This is the only way that we shall have a useful debate; otherwise, it would be only a useless exercise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have made it clear in the past that decisions such as the decision to participate in peacekeeping operations are of such importance that they should be referred to parliament for approval. We therefore welcome the proposed debate on the resolution next Tuesday.
Veterans Land Act
At a time when the Congress of the United States is seeking to assert control of the legislative branch over major international decisions, we in Canada should make it crystal clear that although the initial decision and the negotiation of details rest with the government, the ultimate decision on major issues of foreign policy must be retained by parliament representing the people as a whole. This is essential to the working of parliamentary democracy.
We will leave comment on the decision to participate in the peacekeeping force in support of logistics services and the details of that contribution to the debate when our position can be more fully explained. Suffice it to say that in our view the more hopeful developments in the last few hours in the Middle East would have been impossible without the existence of the United Nations and the willingness of nations to make a contribution to peacekeeping forces.

LACK OF NEWSPRINT SUPPLIES FOR WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that many weekly newspapers in eastern Ontario, some over 100 years old, are being threatened with extinction because of the fact that the pulp and paper industry, and the distributors and suppliers of newsprint, are refusing to supply this basic necessity to the papers concerned, thus creating a situation in which one of the fundamental natural laws of the land, enshrined in the Canadian Bill of Rights, Part I, section 1(f), being "freedom of the press," is put in jeopardy in that there will be no press, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the government not grant any export licences to producers of newsprint, nor allow the selling of Canadian-made newsprint to foreign markets, until supplies of newsprint are guaranteed to all Canadian newspapers, weekly or otherwise, and any other Canadian customers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 26 I ask leave to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the withholding by Canadian manufacturers and distributors of newsprint, the diverting of newsprint to foreign markets, and the failure to guarantee the supply of newsprint by the papermaking and paper distributing companies in Canada to the weekly newspapers of eastern Ontario, thereby constituting a danger to the freedom of the press in that there will be no press in this vital area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be recognized at this stage of the proceedings. I am only sorry that I was not recognized a minute or two ago for a question that I felt was very important to my constituents.
As I began to say on Wednesday in this debate, the bill before us has an underlying objective which all Canadians can support. That objective is the encouragement of Canadians to own Canada, to take up the challenges of developing our own research, to develop in all parts of the country the managerial skills, the research and development facilities and all the domestic infrastructure necessary to enable this country, its people and its commerce to stand on their own feet and be truly Canadian.
In the past, foreign investment has been welcomed and we owe a major proportion of our high state of development and our high standard of living to that fact. Our situation is very similar to that of Australia where the Prime Minister, in a speech to the House of Representatives in that country, said the following:
Overseas capital has played a vital role in Australia's development. It has added considerably to the resources available lor our growth. It has brought with it valuable technological know-how and access to overseas markets. It has created new industries. Australia is a large nation and a prosperous one as a result. The inflow of capital has been associated with increasing overseas ownership and control of industry in Australia. This has been one cost of the increased growth which has come from welcoming overseas capital.
Our experience parallels that very closely. A great deal of foreign investment has entered Canada because the total climate here has been hospitable to it. For precisely the same reason, domestic Canadian investment has also been substantial.
Let us look at what the government is proposing to do in our situation now, with a limited push or a substantial push from the NDP. This country has had a dynamic growth, a growth encouraged by stable government, a
November 9, 1973

satisfactory physical climate and a business climate which has encouraged entrepreneurship. In that regard, the President of Noranda Mines Limited made a speech on October 31, 1973 which I believe is significant. It conveys the attitude that our business community is developing toward the Canadian government. He said:
The reason why Canada has received such a large share of the world's exploration effort-
He was referring to the mining industry.
-has been our hospitable climate towards mining which has led the industry to accept a lower rate of return here than in many other parts of the world. For example, a U.S. government study indicates that average annual earnings on U.S. investment in Canadian mining returned less than 10 per cent from 1954-67 compared with 25 per cent in Latin America. However, we are losing this relative advantage.
Attitudes and proposed legislation with respect to foreign ownership have reduced the amount of non-Canadian capital directed to exploration here, and this trend will likely accelerate. The long period of uncertainty regarding federal taxation policy had an inhibiting effect on the level of exploration activity while the subsequent legislation removing most of the previous incentives has lengthened the odds against finding a commercial orebody. In addition, current attitudes towards mining in certain provinces have had a severe impact on the. level of exploration in large and highly prospective areas of the country.
He goes on to say that industry is facing a number of serious operating problems. He cites labour as being a problem; he cites the heavy capital and operating costs, costs of environmental controls and the incredible inflation which is taking place in construction costs. Those things, Mr. Speaker, are eroding the confidence of not only foreign investors but domestic investors in the future of the Canadian economy. What I understand him to mean is that any company interested in making money for its shareholders, as of course it must be, is no longer looking at Canada. He goes on to say that mining companies are looking at developing nations which are now establishing-and I wish the House would pay attention to this- clear-cut rules for foreign capital. While other nations, competitors of ours for international investment and for Canadian investment, are establishing clear-cut rules, our Canadian government is proposing the fuzziest possible type of legislation.
Whatever became of the idea of calling a spade a spade? Why is it not possible to define some industrial sectors which shall remain under Canadian control? Why can we not say that we welcome foreign investment in designated areas compatible with a generally outlined national industrial strategy? Why can we not develop national industrial rules based on regional and national needs with a voluntary input, a strategy which would enable the government to set out some form of guidelines and firm guidelines that would provide some permanence for both foreign and domestic investors?
This bill does not do that. This bill is not constructive. This bill provides for regulations and control. It intends to rationalize the Canadian industry. It confirms this government's determination to keep on tinkering with what is left of our free market economy until it is totally destroyed. Furthermore, this bill is a measure to provide the executive branch of government with a power to be wielded in a discriminatory, damaging, uncertain and
Foreign Investment Review Act arbitrary manner. It is further evidence to the people of this country, and to the business community, that this government has one firm, unswerving and continuing policy, that is its total devotion to ad hocery. Our party, and specifically my colleague the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), has made amendments to this act which would provide an assurance of input from provincial authorities. Those amendments go some distance toward removing some of the grosser uncertainties. At least a potential investor might be assured that a plan approved by the province had some reasonable chance of avoiding the consequences of the minister's regal whim.
I ask members in considering this bill to consider that we are not a unitary state, that we have regional aspirations, that investment capital does not flow from the financial capitals of this country to the hinterland, as it might. We have differing regional interests within the national framework. In this context, it is not proper to ask provincial governments to forsake their own responsibilities for property and civil rights.
The Canadian Bar Association made a submission to the government with regard to this bill. I do not have the original submission, but I have a quotation from the Financial Post, from an editorial including this paragraph: Indeed, Ottawa is on shaky constitutional grounds on its provisions to restrict sales made to foreigners. As the Bar's brief says, "the right to dispose of one's property is ordinarily within the provincial jurisdiction of the Property and Civil Rights power as enumerated in section 92 of the BNA Act.
There is that consideration which, I believe, adds some uncertainty to the whole impact of this act.
Then, we come to the subject of "significant benefit". The interpretation of the provisions of the bill and of the words "significant benefit" will vary greatly depending on the eye of the beholder. Coming from a region that is one of the have-nots, it will be difficult to convince myself that this government, hived as it is in central Canada, propped up as it is by the NDP which gathers its support from central Canada, can exercise that detached and objective judgment which would be required to administer this power, this power which means development or no development, progress or stagnation in different regions of this country.
Even if the minister is totally fair, totally unbiased, the biggest fault will still remain- the total lack of guidelines. Business is still left to guess whether or not it is safe to move. Uncertainly will be their greatest hurdle. Can we trust this coalition government to make objective decisions in any event? Can we trust them to be fair?

These spokesmen say we cannot. I would remind the NDP that it was the Liberal party in power that established policies whereby foreign investment in this country has reached $60 billion. It has, after all, been in power for the past 75 years with three short breathing spaces. Now, they have had a conversion. They want to buy Canadian.
Furthermore, they say they will be happy to consult, even though the legislation does not require it, with the provinces in these matters. But I ask you: where was consultation over offshore oil rights off the Atlantic coast?

Foreign Investment Review Act Where was consultation with regard to the development of the tar sands? Where was consultation when it was decided by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) to terminate certain fisheries off the Atlantic coast, and where was consultation when the export tax was imposed on crude oil? No, they will not be consulting; they are the government of confrontation.
I was interested in listening to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) on Wednesday. He said we can trust the government. He said that they are more reliable than the provincial governments which are blindly clamouring for industries based on foreign capital. He seemed to feel that foreign investment was tainted in some way, that is unless it was invested in his riding. He comes from an area of Canada where, in all probability, growth will continue by virtue of its own momentum. He complained recently about the failure of the federal government to demand that U.S. companies invest more money in the Canadian auto industry in Ontario. I suspect he might also be favourably disposed to increased tire manufacturing in his area under foreign ownership. But he says no to foreign investment in the Maritimes. If it is a Michelin tire plant or a Volvo automobile plant, where does he stand on that?
As I said a moment ago, significant benefit is all in the eye of the beholder. It is not of any significant benefit to Canada to have the NDP continue to prop up this government in view of the discretionary power given to the minister in this bill and that may well be the cause of the poorer provinces of this country losing industrial opportunity. It is not of any significant benefit to Canada, I submit, to have the Atlantic area continue perpetually to rely on central Canadian manufacturers for its manufactured goods. That may well be the price we pay if this bill passes in its present form.
Speaking of significant benefit a little further, this provision seems to be putting the wagon before the horse. Why should the onus, in determining whether or not it is of significant benefit, be on the investor? Why should he, in effect, be required to enter into the Canadian scene, to orient himself to Canadian commercial and social values to such an extent that he can judge the proposal to be made in terms of whether or not it would be of significant benefit to Canada? Rather, the onus should be on the controlling authority, the onus should be shifted to the government, to the minister, as it is in Australia where a similar type of judgment is made by an independent authority. In Australia, however, having been judged by the independent authority, the investment will be rejected only if it is determined to be against the national interest. It seems that we have the emphasis the other way round.
The adoption of the amendments proposed would go some distance toward removing the most obvious deficiencies in this bill. Providing for a provincial input in itself would ensure some objectivity and give some assurance to the investor as to the considerations to be applied to his application.
There are other actions which the government should be initiating. First, we should consider tax changes to encourage Canadians to invest at home by giving them a competitive edge on foreigners and foreign corporations doing business in Canada; second, tax changes that would make

it more profitable for Canadians to invest in Canada than to invest in the same business in another country.

speechtext:
Third, consideration should be given to rebating capital gains tax when gain is realized from the sale of a business or an industry to another Canadian; fourth, positive encouragement of small business enterprises by utilising tax delay measures similar to the retirement pension programs; fifth, positive encouragement of research and development in this country, possibly by a system of tax exempt profits based on equivalents spent on research or perhaps mining and oil exploration. Sixth, and most important, this government should be taking steps to assure investors, both domestic and foreign, that Canada's laws will not be changed daily, weekly or annually so that any potential investor will know on a long term basis what regulatory controls and tax laws his corporation or business will need to face. Investors should be assured that changes will be taking place in a gradual manner rather than suddenly, overnight.
I conclude as I began by saying that the underlying philosophy of this bill is one which I can happily support, and which I believe most Canadians can support. The methods provided in the bill leave much to be desired. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any doubt in the minds of most members of my party why we, at times, support the Liberal government, particularly in view of the speech to which we just listened. Much has been said with respect to Bill C-132 at report stage, and so I do not wish to take up too much more time at this point in the debate. However, there are a few aspects with respect to foreign ownership and domination of our economy to which I would like to address myself today.
With your indulgence I would like to reflect briefly on some of the historical aspects of foreign domination by drawing a parallel between the great era of industrial development in the United States following the war between the states, and the inflow of foreign, mainly U.S. capital, into Canada in the last two decades.
At the end of the civil war in the United States, businessmen welcomed foreign capital from Europe, and of course for excellent reasons. They needed money in order to build railways, canals, factories and so on. But, Mr. Speaker, they were very careful to make sure that the capital they sought, and indeed got, was bond capital. This meant while foreign capital poured in, the American tycoons had completed control over how the money was to be spent, and foreign investors had no equity voting privileges whatsoever. This, of course, was a real coup for the Yankee robber barons of that period.
Contrast this with the deplorable situation that has been allowed to develop in Canada in the last 20 years,
November 9, 1973

where almost all foreign investment has been in equity voting capital, and where foreign investors simply moved in and, to a great extent, took over our economy. This is why today most of our natural resource industries, and a substantial proportion of manufacturing and food processing industries, are foreign controlled or owned outright. As we all know, Mr. Speaker, the foreign investors are not to blame. They saw a good thing and took full advantage of it. We needed that capital 20 or 30 years ago, but surely the time has come when we must put a stop to any further foreign economic domination, especially when we are now dealing with huge multinational corporations whose power and influence in the world are greater than many nations themselves.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, if we do not now exercise control and restraint over the multinationals, they will soon control us. In some countries this has already happened. I can recall the statements made by the President of Mexico when he spoke to us in this House about a year and a half ago. He called upon Canada to co-operate with Mexico in restraining the fantastic powers of the multinationals, and it was my interpretation that he was referring to those based in the United States because of that country's close proximity to both Mexico and Canada.
I can also recall the number of members from all parties who applauded the Mexican President's remarks with respect to multinationals. So, Mr. Speaker, it is almost too late to regain control of our economy. In the available time left we must make every effort to repatriate our economy so that we will achieve control over our economic and political destiny, bearing in mind that we must co-operate in good faith with other national economies in the interests of greater human development and world peace. This is why my party supports Bill C-132 in principle, although we recognize some very glaring weaknesses in it. In my opinion, the bill is really not tough enough.
Before getting into the specifics of the weaknesses I would like to explode the myth, so common among most Liberals and Conservatives, that we must have foreign investment in order to develop our economy. This might have been true a couple of generations ago, although the inflow should have been bond capital, as I suggested earlier. The fact is that during the 1960's there was a net outflow, in terms of investment, from Canada. During that decade foreign firms operating in Canada sent out of Canada in interest, dividends, royalty fees, management fees and so on over $2 billion more than all the capital they imported. Of all foreign investment every year, only 6 per cent came from foreign countries and 94 per cent came from retained earnings, profits kept in Canada, and funds borrowed from Canadian banks and other financial institutions. In short, Mr. Speaker, we are in the embarrassing situation where we are selling out our own country with our own earned capital.
Contrast this situation with that of Japan. A broken and beaten nation in 1945, Japan struggled with its economy- and U.S. aid-until it has become one of the major manufacturing and trading nations in the world. And while it accepted foreign investment it made it abundantly clear from the beginning that it would be master of its own economic destiny by demanding control over its investment capital, no matter from where it came. And also by
Foreign Investment Review Act contrast, Japan in 1945 was the defeated enemy. Canada and the United States have been friendly neighbours- economically speaking I fear too friendly, but again it is our fault, not theirs. The profits made in our country should not flow out of it through the ominous channels of the multinational corporations. This capital should stay in Canada to develop the private and public sectors of our economy.
Before we quickly condemn the public sector of our economy, let us not forget that our economic development and history have not been the same as those in the United States. In many respects we could not have developed our economy in the 19th century without government aid and intervention. Many capitalists are quick to say, look at the great CPR. What they fail to say is, look at how much public funding was involved in this great enterprise. If you look at tax concessions and give-away land deals, you will see that the success of the CPR was due mainly to government intervention.
Let us look at the present, and at this bill. Let us also look at the reasons for this bill, at long last, being introduced as a much stronger bill that its predecessor which was brought in by the Liberals when they were riding roughshod, with majority government. I can recall the election of 1962 when the Chamber of Commerce published a booklet entitled "People's Capitalism." The Canadian Labour Congress was quick to point out in that election that people's capitalism referred to about 6 per cent of the Canadian public. The other 94 per cent of Canadians were not involved in any way with investment in stocks and private bonds.
From this came an expose on foreign domination of the Canadian economy. All during the 1960's the NDP was the only party that was warning the Canadian public of the consequences of Liberal continentalism, which really meant the big sell-out to powerful multinational corporations to the south. Let me remind this House that a substantial percentage of Americans are opposed to the multinationals as well. The old war cry went up from the Liberals, great and small, that continentalism meant more money coming into Canada, which in turn meant more jobs for Canadians. It was an argument that bought votes, and when it comes to buying votes with the taxpayers' money, the Liberals are absolute geniuses.
But now the chickens are coming home to roost. As long as most Canadians were willing to swallow the Liberal line, nobody in that camp had the guts to tell it as it really was. Oh, there was Walter Gordon and more recently Eric Kierans, but the Liberal party really did not take either seriously-until, of course, last October. Now we have a tougher bill on foreign economic expansion, but a lot is still to be desired. It is very interesting, Mr. Speaker, that a public opinion poll conducted not very long ago indicated that 58 per cent of Canadians favoured the nationalization of our resource industries. I would like to suggest, Sir, that their real motivation was a fear that unless the government stepped in, all our non-renewable resources would be eventually used up, not in Canada's interest but in the interest of foreign corporations and their stock holders.

November 9, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
Bill C-132 has three basic weaknesses, in my opinion. In the first place the proposed legislation is very powerful in that it gives the minister and the chairman of the screening board too much authority to be vested in only two persons. If a minister is genuinely concerned about the harm that continued foreign control of our economy would do, his delegated power could and would, in my opinion, be used wisely to stop further foreign domination. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, if the minister then in office doesn't care about foreign investment, the screening agency would be useless. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these discretionary powers should be vested in an autonomous body of economic experts, well out of the hands of a politician who happens temporarily to be a minister of the Crown.
Second, the bill pertains only to takeovers, new investment and expansion of an existing firm into a non-related area. It says nothing about the expansion of an existing firm into a related area. This is a very important point, Mr. Speaker, because most of the huge foreign corporations we have in Canada can expand easily into related fields since they control so many other companies. For example, ITT controls 58 different companies in Canada. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that if ITT wanted to expand into a non-related field, it could do so through one of its subsidiaries in a related field without having to be screened.
I am also concerned that this bill, because of the confusion that will arise from defining what is related and what is not related, will affect only between 10 and 20 per cent of foreign economic and financial activity in Canada. In other words, as much as 80 or 90 per cent of foreign expansion will probably go unscreened. This loophole should be plugged, so that a company like Gulf Oil cannot expand into the toothpaste business because one of its subsidiaries already manufactures this product.
I am also concerned about one of the amendments now under discussion, specifically one introduced by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), which would give the provinces a powerful voice in the screening process. In this bill we are talking about Canada and foreign economic control, not about one or two of our provinces. I can sympathize with a member who might represent a region or a province where investment capital is badly needed. Surely, it is the role of the federal government to see to it that industry locates in economically slow-growth areas. That is the responsibility of the federal government. I stress that. Let us not Balkanize our country any more than it already is. Let us use Canadian money to develop and expand the economies of slow-growth areas.
In my short speech, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to point out the need to tighten this bill and to impress upon hon. members the need to regain control of our economy, that does not mean that we must try to buy back all industries which are presently foreign owned. I am proposing forward looking policies, so that from now on we will continue to put more and more Canadian capital into Canadian investment and Canadian enterprise.

I am not a chauvinist or a flag waver, but I do have respect for my country. All I ask is that we put our house in order, and a heck of a good way to start is by regaining control of our own economy. At long last the Liberal government has opened its eyes. Let us make sure this is not just another rip-off.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very memorable day, two days before Remembrance Day, for a member of this House to be able to speak on the so-called foreign takeover bill. I firmly believe this affects our beloved country for which so many thousands of our native sons, brothers, fathers, husbands and other relatives died. They wanted to do something to enable Canada to become a nation, so that we could have something here which we could call our own. We have this bill before us, and I think it is a very appropriate time to be able to make a few comments on it.
In 1968, many thousands of Canadians were convinced that with the election of the Liberal government which sits across the aisle, something would be done. There was promise of fortune and fame. Expectations were high. Unfortunately, they let us down. The members of the New Democratic Party are beginning to learn now. Like slithering rats, if I may use that expression, they are leaving the sinking ship. If I may change the analogy, they are like vultures soaring over the carcass of this government that once was. They are now spiralling and soaring because the flesh is flimsy.
I am a rooky. I stand here in the back-most bench. I remember being on the hustings during the election campaign, which was not much more than a year ago. I had very interesting discussions and debates with members opposite and members to my left. Everyone was vying with suggestions as to what should be done to make
Foreign Investment Review Act Canada belong to Canadians again. So, it was with high expectation that I looked forward to the introduction of Bill C-132. But I must confess that when I read that bill disappointment overhwelmed me. My hopes were dashed like a drowned dog. The bill means nothing but high bureaucracy. It is a piece of ad hocery such as the government has always practised when it does not know what to do. I cannot understand why they should not know better because I do not think they are really fools. They are either fools or they lack imagination, and they can let the shoe fit them as they will.
When we speak of foreign takeovers we are concerned basically with United States foreign corporations presently located in Canada who use their retained profits to buy out Canadian industry. Yet we are dealing in this bill with only about 20 per cent of foreign takeovers; 80 per cent are already allowed for under the provisions of the Income Tax Act. The government will not change those provisions. It sits back and wonders why things are going wrong. Surely, they have enough sense to realise that once you permit a foreign corporation to use its surpluses to buy out more and more Canadian business-

speechtext: What is your policy?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I will come to that. Hold on, Buster! They have enacted tax laws which give a break to United States corporations, family corporations, with the result that they are required to pay less income tax than Canadian corporations in the same circumstances. What happens? Of course, Canadian businessmen will sell out to Americans because the Americans can make a better profit and are able to pay a better price. In a negative approach, the kind it so often takes, the government proposes to set up a body of bureaucrats to screen takeover applicants. Isn't that jolly?
But does this give the Canadian people any incentive to invest in their beloved country? I think we have one of the best records for savings per capita of any nation in the industrialized world. But what does the government do to bring out these savings? Where is the incentive? An hon. member asked what I would do. I would change the legislation as it pertains to retained surpluses so that foreign corporations could no longer use those surpluses to buy out Canadian corporations. That is one positive step I would take.
Then, I would give the Canadian people economic incentives to use the savings they have accumulated-give them some Yankee initiative. We could learn a lot from our Yankee friends. They are risking their money. We have more money in our insurance policies and in our savings banks than any country in the western world on a per capita basis. But this government, and the governments which have preceded it, have done nothing to encourage the people to take a chance on Canada. The financial and tax policies of the government do not encourage them to do so. And surely this is the direction in which we ought to be moving, not toward a negative bureaucracy.
I will offer one or two suggestions for hon. members to consider. I might add that I am not pretending to state party policy but just speaking off the top of my head. Why

November 9, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act not say to a United States corporation which has a subsidiary in Canada in the extractive industry: If you intend to operate in Canada, set up your corporation on the basis of public subscription as far as shares are concerned-not a wholly-owned subsidiary, but a public corporation in which Dan Jones and Tim Buck can buy shares. Having brought about a situation in which anyone could buy shares in the corporation, you would then say to the directors: This year you process 10 per cent of your production in Canada and next year you will process 15 per cent. Keep raising the required level. In this way we could build up the secondary industries we so badly need, and those industries would be owned by the Canadian people.
About a year and a half ago the government decided to cut corporation taxes from 49 per cent to 40 per cent. This so-called fiscal policy was designed to deal with the unemployment situation. It has not worked worth a tinker's damn. Yet it should not be difficult. You say to a Canadian corporation: Increase your exports by X factor and we will give you a discount on your income tax accordingly. Doesn't this make sense? Of course, it does. This will encourage people to invest their money in Canada and surely that is the object of the exercise. You would say to a corporation: Increase the employment you provide by a factor of X and we shall cut down your income tax by Y. This would help solve unemployment and the whole of Canada would reap the benefit.
Let me give an example of what the government has done to encourage investment in Canada by Canadian companies. In doing so I should refer to that famous little body known as the Industrial Development Bank. Hon. members talk about $250,000. The average size of a loan made by the Industrial Development Bank in 1972 was $45,000. No takeovers there. In no way would the IDB help Canadians. The Yankee comes up here, goes to our bank and he gets all the money he needs. You know that, Mr. Speaker. But what do the banks say when a Canadian comes in? The answer is, no. Do hon. members realise that 16 per cent of the applicants for loans from the IDB in 1972 did not get a dime? Or that every loan in excess of $100,000 had an interest rate attached to it of more than 10 per cent, though the prime rate charged by the banks in 1972 was 6 per cent? Is this government policy? Is this the way to encourage Canadians to develop and invest in our country? I say it is shameful.
