speechtext:
I will keep it positive. I do not know where the economic policies of this government come from. It must either be from the grave or they have not been born yet.
I have one further brief comment, Mr. Speaker. My colleagues from Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and South Western Nova (Mr. Haliburton) have covered very explicitly and learnedly the problem of the provincial governments to which we have made reference. I support their amendments. I think they are utterly necessary. A judge once said to me: "Trevor, you know where the ivory tower is", and he pointed to his head. We have five basic economic units in this country and, let us face it, Mr. Speaker, no one sitting up in the ivory tower we have here under-

stands the problems of the Maritimes, Saskatchewan and B.C. all at the same time. These people are not gods.
Therefore, let us have a rotating committee if necessary comprised of people who know the problems of a given area. We are now faced with an energy crisis because the government failed to consult. My colleague for South Western Nova mentioned other problems that have arisen as a result of the failure of the government to consult with the provinces. If we believe in federalism, then let us make it work. But it will not work unless this government has the courage, perhaps with some embarrassment, to take its hat in hand and go to the provinces and say: "All right, maybe we were a bit high-handed and have done things that are wrong, but we believe in this federalism bit; let us get together and do the thing properly". That is the attitude the government should take. With a revolving committee examining the problems of an area we will not reach any hidebound or rigid opinions; instead, there will be a flow of personnel going back and forth who represent the various regions of Canada.
The minister said that this would amount to a veto. That is nonsense. It will simply be a case of people consulting one another eyeball to eyeball, and they stay there till somebody winks. This is what is necessary. Certainly, the government's DREE program cannot exist in the present atmosphere. The Maritimes are depressed and need capital, but Canadians are not supplying it. How are the Maritimes going to exist without it? The government must recognize these problems. What may be good for Ontario and Quebec-and I come from Ontario-may not be good for the Maritimes. I say put people from the Atlantic provinces on this committee because they will know how to deal with maritime problems.
In summary, I say the bill is negative. It is a do nothing, too little, too late measure-a cliche, I know, but nevertheless true. The government must realize that not too much time is left on our side, which is why it must be positive. We want positive programs, not negative bureaucracy. Lastly, I say let us have that consultation which is necessary with the provinces and regions so that federalism will mean something to us all.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all indicate my support for this measure. I think it is a much improved bill over the one presented to the previous parliament. Nevertheless, it is a bill with some very great defects, and I regret that the government has not given any indication of willingness to accept the amendments that we have put forward.
Although it can be remedied through political action, I nevertheless want to point out that in its legislative form the bill has a major defect in that it does not deal with reinvestment and the further expansion of foreign ownership in this country. For instance, there is nothing in the present bill to limit the ability of the multinational oil companies to expand their operations. This, to me, is one of the most serious problems facing the country. Admittedly, many of the problems associated with ownership can be dealt with in a political way without legislation. We have had ample evidence that, if the government is prodded sufficiently by the public or by the concerned citizens on this side of the House, then it is able to act. This happened in the case of uranium. Long before this
November 9, 1973

bill, it took action against the oil industry. So, the only hope is that politically some action will be taken.
The oil industry shows the vicious effect that foreign ownership can have on the Canadian economy. I want to add one rider. I am not one who believes that power automatically goes with ownership. In my view, power is political. It is this House of Commons that possesses the power rather than the multinational oil companies. When the House of Commons or the government want to take action, action can be taken.
Nevertheless, if an indictment can be made out against foreign ownership, it is in the oil industry. We might ask ourselves, for instance, would Canada be in the mess it is in today, would it be talking about curtailing energy supplies east of the Ottawa Valley, had the industry been in Canadian hands rather than in foreign hands? I think the answer is a resounding no. We would not have been in the mess we are in today but for the fact that our oil industry is dominated by the multinational corporations.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this calls for an explanation and I shall be very pleased to give one. Let me go back a little and recall that there are two major segments that comprise the oil industry. I should not say two major segments; there is a major segment and a minor segment. The foreign-owned corporations hold about 91 per cent of the assets in the oil and gas industries. The Canadian independents hold the remainder, with the exception of a small percentage that is held under public ownership. The policies of these two groups were diametrically opposed.
The national oil policy of 1961 was written for the benefit not only of Canadian independent oil producers but for the benefit of multinational corporations. The evidence is very clear from the Conservative government of that day that the purpose of the national oil policy of that time, and one which continues to the present, was to assure that the multinationals could manouevre the market to suit their own best interest. To the multinationals, it makes no difference where the money comes from as long as they make the profit. Therefore, we negotiated a deal whereby the multinationals would ship to their subsidiaries in the United States in return for which we would import through subsidiaries in the Quebec area and all eastern Canada, from the same companies. In other words, we would allow the internationals to allocate their reserves where they pleased.
The argument was that it was much cheaper but what was the consequence, Mr. Speaker? The consequence was that a pipeline to Montreal was not built. The multinationals argued that they would rationalize the market internationally. They would ship and refine where they pleased. That was supposed to have been in the best interests of Canada and that was their policy when it came to the development of the oil and gas industry of Canada.
Many of these transactions were not at arms length. The government of British Columbia is still trying to overcome the bad deal made by Westcoast Transmission for gas sales to the United States which many times were made below
Foreign Investment Review Act cost. The sales were made to a subsidiary in the United States or a company that the multinationals were associated with in the United States. They simply allocated the market in this way.
We might ask if things would have been any different if it had not been for foreign ownership. Let us look at the view of the Canadian producers. I was unhappily reminded of this when I attended a meeting recently in Banff where there were some representatives of the Canadian Independent Oil Producers Association. They told me that they had heard our party is now pushing for the Montreal pipeline. We have always pushed for that, Mr. Speaker, but they have just become aware of it. What they were really saying was, "where were you when we needed you". Well, we were there but at that time they were not paying too much attention to us. Rather, the independent oil producers were directing their energies to both the Liberal and Conservative parties in order to persuade them to build the pipeline to Montreal. They needed it because they did not have access to the American market.
Year after year they made their proposals to every member of parliament promoting the building of the Montreal pipeline saying that one day we would be in trouble on the east coast and would need the pipeline. When the oilwells of Alberta were prorated, when they overbuilt and overproduced and the Americans would not take our oil, production was cut back to 35 per cent or 40 per cent but the independents were cut back to 15 per cent or 20 per cent of production so for economic reasons a pipeline had to be built to supply the Canadian market because no other market was available. Unlike the multinationals, the independents could not play games around the world, therefore they had to depend on the Canadian market.
I am not saying for one moment that a Canadian capitalist is that much better than an American capitalist. I have been a socialist much too long to take that view, Mr. Speaker. What I am suggesting is that in this particular case the interests of the capitalists, as I think history will show, coincided with the national interest because they only had one market and they had to worry about that market. They were not diverted by what was happening in Venezuela or the Middle East because they just had this one arena in which to operate.
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that were it not for foreign ownership Canada would not be facing any kind of crisis in terms of supply. The people of Quebec would not be asking themselves whether there is going to be sufficient fuel oil this winter to keep them warm. They would not be running around the world trying to buy tanker cargoes in order that there be some continuity of supply.
We have suffered enormously, but the question must be asked, did we have the money and could we have done it? Of course, we could have done it. At no time, from the figures I have been able to see, has the investment in the oil industry exceeded 4 per cent of the gross national product. Surely, a country that saves almost 25 per cent of its gross national product is in a position to develop these industries. The technology is quite simple. As a matter of fact, virtually all the work in oil development exploration is done by Canadian companies. There is an hon. member

Foreign Investment Review Act in this House who is engaged in drilling operations. The oil company simply acts as the entrepreneur. The technology is available internationally and often the majors themselves bring in specialists. The refineries are designed by specialists who would work equally as well for the Canadian government or entrepreneur as for anyone else.
Then, we may talk about a risk. What sort of risk is involved when there is a market for the product and when you know the product is in the ground? Certainly, you may dig some dry holes but there is no risk. Certainly, if an independent operator can only dig four or five holes and they turn out badly, he is in trouble but the operator who is prepared to keep on digging is eventually going to recoup. I do not know of an instance where a major has gone broke, Mr. Speaker. I know of some independents who have, but you would have to look a long time to find any major oil company that has gone broke because of too many dry holes.
I think we have a clear indication, Mr. Speaker, of the harmful effects, the damaging effects of foreign ownership in the energy industry. That is in the past. Perhaps if there had been foreign ownership 30 or 40 years ago when this business was starting we might not have been any wiser- we might have it permitted it to proceed. But the important thing is not what happened in the past, although it could serve as an illustration of what might happen in the future; it simply means that under no circumstances should there be any expansion in the area of energy by anyone except Canadians. The multinationals must be kept completely out of any further development of our energy resources. This is particularly pertinent because of the tar sands which are now ready for development. We in this party-and I think there are many people across the country not of this party who share the view-think that these tar sands should be developed not only by Canadian ownership but by Canadian public entrepreneurship and that nothing else will serve the national interest but that.
Any provincial-righter who may follow me may comment that the resources belong to the provinces. Of course they are physically in the provinces, and the provinces have a major claim on them, but there is nothing in the suggestion of public ownership that would exclude the provinces from participation. Surely, the federal government and the provinces together should be involved in the planning and development of energy sources in the future.
I should like to point out another reason why I think the multinational oil companies should not be permitted any expansion in the field of energy. Whatever these companies may have paid in the way of provincial royalties up to this point, they have paid virtually nothing in federal taxes-perhaps 2 per cent or 3 per cent. However, for all practical purposes, they have paid almost nothing compared to the manufacturing industries or even the mining industry. Until now the oil companies have taken the position that they have not really taken any money out of the industry; all these years they have been ploughing back earnings and developing the industry, and now they are just reaching the point where their sales are exceeding their expenditures.

While these oil companies are telling us this, they also neglect to tell us that they have 10 billion barrels of oil underground which, even at the controlled government price, is worth $40 billion, that is $40 billion of clear profit they they are ready to extract. They desperately need to go into high capital expenditures in order to avoid paying government taxes. They have reached the point where all the shenanigans will not do them any good and they will have to start paying tax. Nothing is more horrible to a multinational company than the prospect of paying taxes. So now they are coming to the Canadian government and saying we must give them special concessions to go into the tar sands. They say they will develop the tar sands because the incompetent Canadians will never be able to do it by themselves. They need the tar sands even more than we need the tar sands. They have to find some way of increasing their capital cost, of increasing the development and expenditure costs in order to cut down on their tax liabilities.
I do not think these multinational oil companies should be permitted to do that because, as I said earlier, they have really damaged the national economy in the most profound way and they are using it as a way of avoiding the payment of taxes. I think we have every reason to be suspicious and concern about foreign ownership in this particular case. I have been concerned about foreign ownership throughout this debate and over the last number of years. The difficulty with the debate is that foreign ownership was debated almost entirely on moral grounds, on so-called nationalistic grounds, on what I call Walter Gordon grounds. I think Walter Gordon is a great man, but in this sense he proved himself to be too great a moralist because the approach he took was that if we get rid of foreign ownership we will be somewhat poorer for it. He accepted the idea that foreign ownership made us richer, when in fact it is not true at all.
Foreign ownership and foreign investment have made us poorer. Walter Gordon took that argument as a point of departure and said to Canadians: Look, it will reduce our standard of living, but surely it is worth it in order to recover our manhood. He put it on that basis. This reminds me of the thinking of some of the old CCF'ers. I wonder how we missed out on Walter Gordon. He has a marvellous mind, but this was a faulty premise and one he never should have adopted. Unfortunately, Canadians came to believe it. They have been taking the attitude: we acknowledge that if we clamp down on foreign ownership we will become poorer; nevertheless, it is worth it because we want to be an independent nation, we want to find our own way, we want to express our manhood or womanhood, as the case may be. But in fact we have lost out both ways. We lost our independence and our economy has suffered as a result of foreign ownership.
Unfortunately, the time available to me today does not permit me to speak about other industries under foreign ownership. I believe I could make quite a good case to show that whatever industries foreign ownership has touched, those industries have been lucky to have survived. Without foreign ownership, this country would have been infinitely better off, both materially and spiritually. We could have accommodated Walter Gordon
November 9, 1973

and people like myself. Today my point is to make the argument that if we are going to have a national policy on energy that will serve the interests of this country, foreign ownership must be excluded.
I would like to read an excerpt from a report prepared by the research and development department of the Canadian National railroad in September 1962. It is entitled: "Some Implications of Marketing Canadian Crude Oil in Montreal". This refers to what I said earlier about the desire of independent oil producers to build a pipeline to Montreal. All kinds of studies were carried out around that time to see how feasible the building of that pipeline would be. In the chapter of this report entitled "Political Implications" at page 20 what emerges is that the pipeline was not built because of political blackmail from the multinational corporations and from the countries with which they were associated. I would like to quote directly from this report. It reads:
Reaction to the pipeline, and to the resulting exclusion of Venezuelan and Middle East oil from the Quebec market by means of controls on imports, might be expected from many quarters: from the exporting countries which supply Canada; from the international oil companies, largely owned and controlled in the U.S.; from U.S. independent producers; from the U.S. federal government; and from such international organizations as the OAS and GATT.
One wonders, today when those east of the Ottawa Valley line are facing what might be a hard winter, where GATT is to help us out and where the international oil companies are to help us out. They are not around. These were the groups that apparently counselled that if Canada were to build the pipeline to Montreal and attempt to make itself self sufficient in energy, then international repercussions and censure would follow. I do not think that the CNR is a terribly radical organization, and it is not worthwhile going beyond the paragraph that I quoted because the rest of it merely confirms, enhances and enlarges upon what I have said.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate on Bill C-132, to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons, one knows from the outset that basically this debate has gone on in this country for the 100 years that this country has established itself north of the 49th parallel. The debate on foreign ownership, Canadian independence and Canadian identity is as old as this country. But this does not make the debate any less relevant. The problem in this debate, and its relevancy, is the bill under discussion, and I wonder about it because we are all nationalistic. There is not a thought in this bill, however, with which any member on any side of the House can disagree. We all want to be Canadians.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I agree with the parliamentary secretary to the minister and I echo him en frangais or en anglais.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Bravo.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
We can all preach, sermonize and philosophize about being Canadian and we all try to preempt
Foreign Investment Review Act members in other parties with regard to what party is the most Canadian. However, I do not want to indulge in that type of rhetoric here this afternoon at the end of a busy week by suggesting that it was the Conservative party around 100 years ago, which, through consultation and co-operation with some elements of this land mass north of the 49th parallel, developed and defined this country which is now known as Canada. This was not accomplished through confrontation, or gimmickery, or floss- and basically this bill is floss. I wonder if one day the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) will be so against foreign ownership that he will want the International Nickel Company to close down its smelters in Sudbury, putting him out of a job and leaving his constituents without anything in their pocketbooks. That is the type of shallow hypocrisy that comes from those to my left, those who preach pan-Canadianism. Just think of how Canadians sometimes are deluded by the CBC or by some of the PR management consultants working for the government.
Where Bill C-132 is on the side of all the angels is in its principle of trying to do something for Canada. But where we differ from time to time, depending on were we sit, is whether this bill is really going to do the things which obviously the minister thinks and hopes it will do. But before I come to the bill itself, Mr. Speaker, before we get caught up in the rhetoric of nationalism, and "Are you a good Canuck"? may I ask who the heck has been in charge of this country for the last 50 years but the Liberal party, except for 11 beautifull breathing years when this party formed the government.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man), who is one of the more imaginative, respectable, venerable, and now perhaps retiring members of this House, speaks so knowledgeably about oil and gas when talking of the energy problems facing the country. I can understand his propensity for gas, although I do not always agree with him on oil. He speaks sincerely about the problems facing this country in the energy field during the coming cold winter. And then we hear the platitudes from across the way about nationalism.
This parliament will be terminated when those who sold their philosophical soul for a mess of political pottage finally wake up to the realization that they are on a dead-end street. Who is going to vote for the NDP in the next election? We all know that NDP meant in the days of Mr. Coldwell and Mr. Douglas. It meant New Democratic Party, and before that the Commonwealth Co-operative Federation. Today NDP stands for "No Damned Principle." That is what it means, and the NDP are on a deadend street, because in the next election Canadians will have a choice between either the government or opposition parties.
I do not stand here today and say that the opposition has all the answers or has that connection with the Divine that makes it infallible. We do not, but we can rest easy that the next general election will not be polluted with the charade of a party masquerading under the name NDP when that party has no damned principles. Some 39 of the last 50 years have been years of Liberal rule, not the classical rule of the old Liberals like the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), not the classical rule of the
7714

Foreign Investment Review Act Liberal party of Mr. St. Laurent and other great Liberals who contributed much to this land. Today the President of the Treasury Board may be the last Grit about whom one can draw an analogy with the movie titled "True Grit." The present Liberal party does not have policies. It is built on sandstone. I think it was the man from Toronto, Blake, who founded the Liberal party, who coined the name Grit. He said, "We are as strong as grit." The present Liberal party stands on swamp, supported by the NDP.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Supported by swamp gas.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know you wish me to speak on the bill, and I am coming to that, but I just wish to define the atmosphere in which we are debating Bill C-132. Was it Saul or Paul who took that journey on the road to Damascus?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Saul.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Thanks very much. Anyway the Middle East is very much to the fore these days, but never has there been such a conversion on that road to Damascus as has happened to the party opposite, the sandstone Grits. They finally realize there is a problem about the ownership of Canada, after having sold our birthright for economic pottage, for a few dollars from below the border and across the seas. Now, they try to pretend that this bill will solve the fundamental problem of foreign ownership.
How can we have a bill defining guidelines on economic nationalism when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has stood in his place many times and refused to define something called a "Canadian industrial strategy"? How can you have a bill on economic nationalism which avoids and almost eliminates any consultation with the provinces that make up the flesh of this skeleton known as Canada? In all seriousness, this is a fundamental flaw, Mr. Speaker.
Now, I come to the other fundamental flaw. There is something in this bill called a foreign review takeover agency. I am glad the hon. member for Nickel Belt understands what it is. I tell him he could be confronted with some speeches of his old leader, who was a great leader. The present leader is like a chameleon; he changes according to the colour of the day. In the old days when the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan The Islands (Mr. Douglas) talked about Tweedle-Dum and Tweedle-Dee he made some sense, but now we have Tweedle-Dum over here and Ho-Hum over there. That is the main problem.
But returning to the bill, which I know you want me to do, Mr. Speaker, and to the amendments, I would have thought the bill came from the hand of the President of the Treasury Board rather than from the hand of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce because it is so managerial, so bureaucratic in scope that one finds it almost impossible to imagine what could conceivably happen.
I say this because not too many years ago in an earlier debate which the President of the Treasury Board will remember-I think he was a deputy minister at that time-there was great controversy over a definition in the Customs Tariff Act which gave some discretion to the minister of national revenue or the minister of finance in

interpreting something called "class or kind." I will attempt to educate the hon. member for Nickel Belt on this, if possible. In the discussion on class or kind, members of the then opposition, led by the four horsemen, Pickersgill, Chevrier, Mr. Pearson and the present government leader in the senate, Senator Martin, for day after day castigated the government and criticized and complained about the arbitrary, discretionary power that was to be given to the then minister of national revenue in interpreting the meaning of "class or kind", as applied to goods entering Canada: he could decide whether those goods or products were of a class or kind made in Canada. That was an arbitrary discretion to be exercised by the minister.
Under the act, the minister could exact tariffs which would prevent certain goods entering this country and thereby help industry in Canada to grow. That is what the government of the day wanted. The opposition complained that the then minister of national revenue in the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was to be given dictatorial powers. The minister was to decide matters for which there were no guidelines, no rules and no regulations. He would interpret these things according to the functioning of his digestion or his indigestion, as the case may be, and make interpretations with regard to class or kind.
What those members said in 1961, more than ten years ago, about the discretion of the minister could be said with even more conviction today. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce does not need to take the advice of the foreign takeover advisory council. The minister has power to decide if foreign capital coming to this country will be of significant benefit to Canada, and he can decide this without guidelines, terms of reference, rules or regulations, according to his indigestion, good humour or, hopefully, good sense. He must make the decision.
There is a place in Nova Scotia called Point Tupper which has delivered to it oil from offshore. That is the only place where we can now get oil, the offshore mineral rights question not having been finally settled. Quebec wants to define what is an oil superport. Unless some protection is built into the act, as suggested in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and other amendments which the House will consider, and unless the provinces are given the opportunity to provide meaningful input and engage in consultative procedures and processes, it is possible that the sort of deep water port contemplated at Point Tupper will be built elsewhere. Unless we are able to provide some meaningful and substantive input with respect to consultations with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as to what foreign capital will be of significant benefit to Canada, it is possible that such deep water ports may be developed in other parts of Canada. I hear that especially Ontario and Quebec want a deep water port.
You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that a political battle is being waged right now on where the next nuclear heavy water plant is to be developed in Canada.

Obviously, this is Friday afternoon generosity. I do not intend to expand my remarks further and go into any detailed dissection of the bill. I merely say that no good will come of this bill until the government decides to bring in an industrial strategy and take part in meaningful consultations with the provinces. After all, a country is made up of many parts, just as a man is. I am a man of many parts; I have legs, arms, and so on. We are a people of many parts and we make up the political life of this land. Canada is only as strong as the provinces which make up the parts.
I have very great respect for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as a person, but as a minister he is just learning. I notice that the government whip has said something. He is becoming more of a "whipper". He knows a good deal about the machinations of members, because in this House he is a man of experience. The minister, too, is gaining experience, I suggest to the minister that he has much to learn about trade and commerce, and we shall only make progress if we include the provinces in a consultative role. We are not reassured by the examples of consultation which have taken place with respect to taxes, with respect to oil and gas policies, feed grains policies and social policies. We are not that simple even though certain people may think we are.
We are the ones who in the last election said that one of our first items of priority when we obtained power-and we have only been thwarted in one way-would be to have a federal-provincial conference to try to define for the people of Canada the national priorities. That type of consultative role would have helped.
I am a little involved in communications policy because my leader said that this is perhaps one area where one could be challenged. I know I am getting away somewhat from the bill, but I want to say that whether it is on energy or some other area, the word "communications" connotes conversation and consultation. The Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) is not in the chamber, so I will not say anything about him personally. However, I will say something about him as a minister. Three years ago in a Speech from the Throne the government said it would define and develop a communications policy. For three years there has been a tax against the province of Quebec because in February, 1971, their minister, Mr. L'Allier tried to find a communications role for that province.
The second province that got into the act was Ontario. The Ontario minister of transportation and communications, Mr. Carton, defined where he felt Ontario should fit
26635-57 (

Foreign Investment Review Act into the national policy. He was followed by the Alberta minister. Then the new government-and they deserve full credit in British Columbia, where I practised law for six years-appointed Mr. Strachan as minister of communications and he is attempting to find a policy.
In this area, where there should be the greatest consultation and communication, there has been a physical vacuum: there is a fundamental, metaphysical and physical vacuum in any policy between the federal and provincial governments. After being urged by the provincial ministers of communications and some ministers on his side, the federal Minister of Communications is finally going to get the provinces together for a conference. Again, that is not the type of consultative role that we think the provinces should play in this country. The strength of this country depends on, and is defined by, how loud the provincial consultative voice can be heard.

They approach me as a member of parliament from the area and ask me for help, for contacts in the region, and for help at the government level in the form of a grant or loan. We have received some very good government programs.
When I speak to these people, I go beyond the criteria that are set out in this bill. In my constituency there is a large amount of unemployment and poverty. I ask them about the degree and significance of participation by Canadians in business enterprise, about the effect of acquisition on productivity and industrial activity, about the effect of competition and compatible policies. I have had people from Germany and Japan representing certain interests who have asked me for help, and I have said I would help them so long as they obtained supervisory personnel who were bilingual and from the area. In 1971, Triton Industries developed a radio of considerable value to RCMP, air-sea rescue, fishing boats, etc. In April of 1971 it was advised by the Department of Transport that Triton would be placed on a suppliers' list and would be considered when this type of equipment was required.

Let us put in sound working principles and let us recognize the weaknesses we all have and the capacity for error which exists in any administrative system. Let us shore-up the bill. subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider developing an integrated approach to social and economic policy development in Canada through the creation of an economic and social council to establish a more beneficial relationship between the social interests and the business interest in the community in order to help all our institutions be more responsive toward the interests and aspirations of the individual citizen.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I am proposing to the House would provide a way to increase livability in Canada. I am asking that the government provide a structure for social planning through a social council of Canada in the same way that it provides a structure for economic planning through the Economic Council of Canada; and, further, that it integrate economic and social planning in the interest of the total human being.
My motion is aimed at improving the quality of life in Canada not in a vague, motherhood spirit but in a concrete proposal. The social council I envisage would help us to analyse and improve our progress in those areas that are regarded internationally as social indicators of the quality of life. These are: health, individual development through learning, employment and quality of working life, leisure, command over goods and services, physical environment, personal safety and the administration of justice, and social opportunity and equality.
Just as the government is aided in setting economic policy by the thinking and by the excellent reports of the Economic Council of Canada, so it would be helped by the social thinking of the council I propose. Social policy traditionally takes a back seat to economic policy. But the upheavals in modern society demand that we revise and upgrade our way of making social policy.
Since we have long suffered from the compartmentaliza-tion of man, I suggest that the economic and social proposals of the two equal bodies be linked, such as by the issuance of a joint annual report, so that the government receives integrated proposals designed for people. Such comprehensive planning is a vital first step if we are to protect human values in a society already dominated by the computer and soon to be challenged by the genetic engineers.
Let me state briefly why we must bring this new dimension of planning into government. In the development of Canada so far, the accent has been on building and growth. Our success has been measured in the production of goods and services. There has been an assumption that the emphasis on quantity would improve the quality of our life. I am not necessarily critical of this assumption; the material development of Canada has required concentration on the GNP. But the conditions of modern society have changed dramatically in the past few years as a result of the technological and cultural explosions. The intense problems of future shock have hit Canadians. Change used to be gradual but now it is rapid and escalat-
November 9, 1973

ing, allowing us very little time to adapt. The world is changing faster than we can cope with it.
Technology has brought many benefits-communications and transportation are just two examples- but it has also been a chief source of the anxiety and spreading frustration that characterize modern life. The acquisition of more goods has not by itself made us a happier people.
Our economy must grow at 7 per cent a year to maintain progress, as we have traditionally defined that word. This growth rate demands escalating consumer consumption. Thus, increasing numbers of people feel caught up in the faster-turning wheels of progress with no sense of purpose other than growth itself. We have to ask ourselves in this parliament a fundamental question: Is bigger, better? That question deserves the attention of parliament. It deserves much more attention than we have been giving it, for if bigger is better, why are five million Canadians still living below the poverty line? Why has crime increased? Why are alcohol, drug and suicide rates up? Why is there more pollution of water and air? Why is there more labour strife? Why are we congesting in urban areas, leaving vast areas of Canada empty?
These basic questions reveal why the assumptions and patterns of the institutions in our society need re-examination. It is critical that this re-examination take place now because as a result of technology we are entering a new period of our history, a period in which we have acquired the power to shape our own future for better or for worse. We must either control it for the better or it will control us for the worse.
Consider what is happening in our world. We have manned satellites riding the gravitational fences of our planet. We have put men on the moon. We have communications satellites to let us see by live television what is happening on the other side of the world, and sensory devices in orbit to detect and map biological and mineral resources concealed from the human eye. We are entering the bioengineering age in which we can manipulate the nature and structure of living things. Indeed, as Lord Ritchie-Calder of the Centre for the Study of Democratic Institutions maintains: "The whim of the present generation can determine the character of remote posterity." This is more than spare-part surgery or organ transplants; we can tamper with the genetic code and thus produce deviations whose consequences may be unpredictable and irreversible.
I have used this example only to illustrate my contention that we have entered a profoundly new period in our history. It is in these changed circumstances that government policies must be made. Government controls the economy and thus influences the framework of society within which people live their lives. The size and extension of government today makes it a dominant influence on the direction of society. William Dyson, executive director of the Vanier Institute of the Family, puts his finger on our dilemma as follows:
The issue is not that Canada has insufficient wealth... The central problem is people, not dollars: people being increasingly excluded from access to our riches, while a few others here and abroad, are increasingly favoured. Even worse, it is the exclusion of these people-who grow in number and now include business-
Economic and Social Council
men, scientists and engineers-exclusion from work, from status, from identity, from meaningful living.
Despite the enormous and, in some cases, threatening advances of technology, government policy-making and forecasting is still lamentably weak. It is not necessary to reject economic growth to recognize that we have produced wantonly and without recognizing the social impact of our affluence. It is not necessary to dismiss material comfort to recognize other values that are essential to the human and humane qualities of men. Government cannot escape its obligation to take a broad, long view. It must strive to combine economic development and personal well-being. Affluence makes sense only if it leads to increased social justice and personal fulfilment. In this way, economic growth may become a means to the end of an enhanced quality of life.
There are growing voices in Canada today calling for this new emphasis on integrated social planning. Foremost is the Canadian Council on Social Development, the closest body we now have to the model I propose. The council is a private organization drawing its support from the federal government, the ten provincial governments, the 70 largest municipalities and many businesses. Its central objective is social policy development. It does a fine job, but because of its non-governmental status and limited resources it is a poor cousin to the prestigious Economic Council of Canada. The federal government has put $3,-
474,000	into this year's Economic Council budget. The Canadian Council on Social Development has to scrape up its $820,000 annual budget of which $275,000 is contributed by the federal government.
I want to emphasize that keeping social policy as a residual aspect of economic policy is old-fashioned thinking and has led to the chaotic situation in Canada today in which government at all levels spends $6 billion a year on welfare and yet has not significantly alleviated poverty. Our reluctance to put social policy on the same level as economic policy fails to recognize that social policies can be dynamic, lead to incentive and thus, to tax reductions.
A practical benefit of linking economic and social interests is seen in minimum wages, for increasing minimum wages is essential to social advancement. Thus, people are given money for work done, not subsidized for work not done. Instead of collecting extra tax dollars for so many welfare plans, the government could reduce taxes so as to offset increased costs due to higher minimum wages. An increase in minimum wages actually costs the country less because it cuts down on welfare costs. We would then be paying people, not governments. Accordingly, the executive director of the Canadian Council on Social Development, Reuben Baetz, is himself a proponent of an integrated approach to social and economic policy development. Mr. Baetz says:
Canada desperately needs an independent organization active in the formation and promotion of sound social policies. Such an organization must have enough financial support to operate with a high degree of professional competence. It must take into account the needs, resources and attitudes of individual citizens and their organizations in development of policy proposals, but it must avoid becoming the mouthpiece of one or more special interests. It must speak courageously of values and desirable social objectives, but remember that resources are not unlimited ... It must remain non-partisan in politics but skilled in the dynamics and work of
7724

November 9, 1973
Economic and Social Council
the political arena, for that is where all public social policy is finally decided.
Such a model should be created by the federal government in co-operation with the provincial governments. Ad hoc consultations between federal and provincial ministers, while useful, are not good enough because they are dependent on political timing and good will. A permanent structure is needed. Perhaps the Canadian Council on Social Development could provide the nucleus for the model I propose. In any event, this new body should collaborate closely with the Economic Council in the development of social indicators that provide hard data on the quality of life issues.
The Economic Council has also shown increasing interest in the social and institutional aspects of economic development. In its eighth annual report the council noted:
... In our increasingly complex, interdependent society, short range and ad hoc responses to the problems of growth and change seem increasingly inappropriate in many instances.
Several departments of the federal government now look upon social indicators as a necessary instrument of public policy, but their work is fragmented. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion, for example, is developing indicators to measure the problems of social adjustment created by regional economic development. The Department of Labour is conducting research on indicators of job satisfaction. The Science Council of Canada and Environment Canada are both interested in social indicators of the environment. The Department of Health and Welfare's working papers on social security in Canada, focusing on the best method of achieving security of income for all Canadians, are useful as an indication of one important factor contributing to quality of life.
Statistics Canada is currently working on a report of salient trends in Canadian society including population, health, education, income and expenditure, welfare and social security, labour force and employment, leisure arts and culture, justice, housing, environment and urban statistics, participation, opportunity, accessibility and social mobility. This information will provide the basis for judging our "livability index". But we need more than statistical tools to tell us about the quality of our society. A social council is needed to encourage and to integrate such research into proposals for public policy.
Data gathering and analysis would be futile without a corresponding ability in parliament to evaluate proposals. So I come finally to how parliament itself will respond to the information and analyses presented to it. I believe there is an essential role for parliament in judging how the values of our society are being affected by change. In this light, human values need to be reaffirmed. We are not without human concern in our institutions, but we express it in the wrong way. We add on humanizing factors to public policy rather than developing policy that starts from the base of the human being, his rights and dignity. Our social security policies in pensions and unemployment insurance allocations are a prime example of this "adding on" humanization. We create a system which generates casualties and then add on another huge system to compensate the casualties. We must instead make our society conform to our own long-range human needs.

To take another example, our environmental dilemma is but a symptom of a much deeper problem facing us. No one decided to dehumanize life with crowding, traffic jams, noise and squalor. No one decided that air pollution and dying waterways should be the price of unlimited growth. No one decided these things, but neither were they accidents. They are what we have done because we have assumed, unconsciously, that we had the right, indeed the obligation, to do them.
We must begin to see ourselves no long as conquerors, exploiters or plunderers of our planet, but as stewards or trustees of its generous but not unlimited resources, of its resilient but not indestructible systems that support all life. As Maurice Stong, executive director of the UN environment program, explains:
We must begin to see that even if we win the fight against pollution, what will that gain us if three decades from now at least half of humanity will still endure a life of intermittent work, permanent undernourishment, poor health, poor housing and, at present standards, relatively growing illiteracy and lack of skills? Will that be an environment that is human or endurable?
Not only the quality of life in Canada, but global stability demand a reassertion of human dignity to ensure the survival and well-being of the whole human community. A commitment to true humanism does not demand uniformity in our individual or community lives. However, it provides the framework for man's search for beauty and truth, for moral and spiritual growth, and it is in this search that we achieve our highest levels of humanity.
To summarize, we are in an age in which we are transforming our lives and our world. We have done so hitherto on the basis of incomplete knowledge and narrow ambition, principally economic. We must broaden our knowledge and our values to recognize and to enhance the whole man and mankind. To do so we need better social data and analysis to be provided by a social council of Canada.
We must ask ourselves in parliament how we can truly help growing numbers of Canadians who are vulnerable to the economic system and dependent on government programs to gain greater control over their own lives and destiny. Upgrading social policy is the route to a more human society.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much impressed with the speech of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). I could not agree with him more that we as a nation, and perhaps as a whole western European society if we consider ourselves as such, have in the past generation or so been far too concerned about economic growth and not nearly enough about the effects it has on people.
This is not the gist of my speech, because I planned to go into something quite different, but I am particularly concerned about the notion of growth versus the environment. One member earlier gave the example of James Bay. We have to learn how to internalize some of these external costs such as environment and social costs when we get into massive growth schemes. James Bay has to be one of them. The cost in terms of environment, disrupting the Indian people, and so on, has not been internalized. That must be done.
November 9, 1973

I agree with the hon. member that there is a real gap between economic and social planning. This parliament and this government is slowly moving toward a position of greater integration. The key factor in this kind of integration is perhaps the impact on spending for social services, health, welfare, unemployment, family allowances, old age pensions, veterans pensions, disability pensions, the Canada Pension Plan, and so on. There is a whole raft of related welfare services which account for approximately two-thirds of federal government spending. The impact of very heavy spending in this area on the part of the federal government, as well as provincial and municipal governments, is certainly immense in terms of the over-all economic affairs of Canada. It involves a cause and effect relationship that deserves some consideration.
Basically, social needs in an economic sense can be divided into two areas. First, the needs of all citizens, whether they are partaking actively in the economic life of the nation in the sense of being breadwinners and not dependent on the state. These social needs include education, health services and some allowances such as family allowance. In many ways, the more affluent in our society receive a greater share of this kind of welfare than do the poor. Education is a good example. In many ways, it is the affluent who are the welfare bums in the sense that children from affluent families spend many more years receiving expensive education in universities where the staff-pupil relationship is very low and equipment is very expensive. In many ways, the affluent in our society benefit more from the state in terms of welfare than the poor.
The second group of welfare recipients are the needy. These people are dependent because they do not receive an adequate income and must have assistance from the state. This group includes welfare recipients, people on unemployment insurance, people with disabilities, and so on. They are unable to function on their own.
These are the two main groups of welfare recipients in our society. Unfortunately, the latter group seems to come off much worse than the former. Even in areas like health services the latter group does not avail itself. There are many reasons for this. It is possibly because they cannot get babysitters and this sort of thing. A report by the single-parent mothers indicates that these people do not or are not able to avail themselves of health services even though they may be free. Possibly there are also some social reasons.
Planning for social assistance to the second group also has a significant impact on our economy. In a rapid-growth type of society we are very dependent on an affective demand for goods and services. In addition to the supply and humanitarian demands, assistance to this group plays a very significant role in stimulating our economy. Since such groups are not likely to be involved in savings, a steady cash flow is very necessary, especially at times when there may not be very happy consequences with regard to savings and investment.
I can offer an admirable example of the integration of social and economic forces in our national life by referring for a moment to the LIP program. This is not a program
Economic and Social Council
which has a massive impact on our society but it is interesting because of the interaction between social and economic forces. It was designed originally for two purposes, to create jobs and the stimulation of the economy. I would refer to the OFY program in the same category. A third factor has been introduced by the nature of the projects themselves and the scheme has become heavily involved in social service programs. Projects were started as means of creating jobs and ended up as social services and meeting social needs which had been present all along.
The government is concerned about this interrelationship between the social planning side of our national life and the economic side. Serious discussions are going on in the area of finding employment, on the one hand, and the need for compiling inventories of community work so that should unemployment increase, these tasks can be undertaken. Economic necessities affecting social policy, decisions concerning the lowering of pensionable age, and so on, have obvious repercussions on social policy. For example, it seems to me that one of the ways in which we might increase the number of jobs available would be to lower the retirement age.
There are three bodies which deal with planning in Canada in this field, that is, economic and social planning. I have mentioned one, the Economic Council of Canada, and I shall mention another, the Institute for Research on Public Policy. I should also mention the Canadian Council for Social Development, a group which is functioning extremely well though it could function a great deal better if it were possessed of adequate funds. I believe there is much to be said for these groups all getting together to develop integrated policies.
I should like to deal in the few minutes left to me with a subject which concerns me a great deal, that is to say, the whole notion of adversary procedure, an extremely important notion and one which has become better received in the last six months or so, particularly on the Ottawa scene. I am concerned that very often in policy-making there should be massive economic forces aligned against extremely weak social forces. Perhaps this is one of the difficulties which the social council faces-it does not possess the political or economic strength to do the things it needs to do.
Then, again, parliamentary or regulatory bodies tend to be awed by prestigious information; if information is expensively put together we tend to be much more impressed by it than by material put out on behalf of groups which barely have sufficient funds to get them to Ottawa. Nevertheless, it is these groups which often have a great deal to say about the needs of individuals and communities in the social policy field. Perhaps parliamentarians and others concerned should make funds more readily available for such groups to present their cases, particularly where they affect social needs.
One or two examples come immediately to my mind; for instance, groups concerned in an adversary way about decisions to go ahead with pipeline development. Something must be done to ensure a better balance between the various elements in our society, those which have massive economic power and those which are calling attention to pressing social needs.

Economic and Social Council
May I say, in conclusion, that I support the intention behind this motion. I believe the development of a single body to co-ordinate planning in the areas of social and economic affairs is badly needed in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all too often very worth-while ideas are put forward during private members' hour in the form of resolutions and bills, and all too frequently they are rejected by the government. Such an idea is expressed in the resolution put forward today by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). It is, as the cliche goes, an idea whose time has come. All it really does is call upon the government to give consideration to the advisability of setting up a social council of Canada. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona certainly put forward eloquently and sincerely some sound arguments to support his case that there is a need to set up such a council.
I believe the motion should commend itself to the government. All too often we as parliamentarians either on the government side or in the opposition vote public funds to carry out projects in various parts of the country without paying any regard to the social consequences of what we are doing. For example, there is the trend toward vacating the family farm and the movement of people toward the urban centres of Canada. We do not really know in any great depth what are the social consequences of the move toward urbanization in Canada, but we do know to a certain extent what impact it has had upon the rural population who suddenly find themselves placed in an urban milieu.
The obvious example that comes to mind is the resettlement program that was carried on in the province of Newfoundland. This was a program conceived-ill-conceived, in my view-by bureaucrats and technocrats who, in putting together a regional development program for the province of Newfoundland, came to the conclusion that there were too many villages in the province, that there were too many settlements or outports as they are called.
This prompted a decision to reduce the number of settlements in the province and to move the people there into what were called receiving centres. In other words, certain areas of the province were designated for resettlement and other areas for receiving centres or growth centres. People from five or half a dozen small outports would be resettled into a larger community within the area. In the process they were forced to abandon their homes, their fishing premises, their small gardens, schools and churches, all of the things that were familiar to them, the infrastructure that they had built up through the years and which had been passed on from generation to generation.
This move was made without any regard for its social impact. As a result, we saw the very sad spectacle of hardy fisherfolk being placed in these reception centres which gradually became welfare ghettoes. These people lost their small gardens, their little churches and schools and public centres, and as a result lost their sense of being, their sense of belonging and sense of pride. The psychological consequence of this was that they suddenly lost their initiative or urge to work and became wards of the state.

In many cases, they had no choice. They had left their villages, their fishing premises and their traditional fishing grounds, and the places they were sent to were designed, not to provide them with work but as places where welfare and social assistance could be conveniently administered. In my view, it was for the convenience of bureaucrats that this ill-conceived resettlement scheme was carried on.
I am pleased to say it has now been stopped because of the consequences which became apparent after the program was well under way. All these pitfalls could have been avoided if there had been the proper approach made and the kind of study conducted that could be conducted by a social council of Canada. That is about the best example I could give, Mr. Speaker, for supporting the very excellent idea that has been put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.
The hon. member on the other side who just resumed his seat referred to some statistics released by Statistics Canada relating to the low incomes of single-parent families in Canada-the working mothers of this country. This leads me to another question which sooner or later will have to be faced up to, and that is the need to recognize that in this country there are single-parent families that should be given some degree of equality of opportunity. In order to provide them with this equality of opportunity and to provide these women with at least a reasonable return for their labours, we should consider establishing a federal day-care centre program. This, in my view, is long overdue. Such a program could be very conveniently worked out with the provinces and I am sure all provinces would be receptive to the idea.
A social council of Canada would be able to provide us with the necessary information as to exactly how much is involved in such a program and what are the benefits that would flow from a program of this kind. I have one day-care centre in my own city which was started as a consequence of the Local Initiatives Program. Most of the children in that day-care centre are from families which are on social welfare and which take advantage of the day-care centre to enable the parents to enter the work force and supplement their welfare payments. A great number of the children come from homes where the father has deserted the family and the mother has had to go out to help supplement her welfare payments in order to keep the family going.
The fact that this one day-care centre in a city of 100,000 people had to be started under the Local Initiatives Program points up, to my mind, the fact that here is where we as legislators are falling behind in keeping pace with the need for social development in this country. Social development, as the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona said, and said so eloquently and sincerely, should go hand in hand with and be complementary to the economic development of this country; because to my mind to have one without the other is to invite disastrous consequences.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first had the opportunity of looking over the motion proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) I said to myself, "This strikes me as being an excellent idea". As is my habit, I then began to examine the resolu-
November 9, 1973

tion to see whether any of its components already existed in Canadian society today. As I began to think about his resolution, it became clearer and clearer to me that what he was really seeking to do was to create an institution known as the House of Commons. Because in point of fact, the role which the hon. member has outlined for his proposed new body is exactly the role which the House of Commons fulfils. It is this body which is the co-ordinator, and ultimately the final law-giver, in dealing with the kind of problems the hon. member suggested might be looked after by another institution or organization. For what is the House of Commons if it is not a body that deals with economic and social problems?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: This House has not been doing it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
If the House of Commons has not been doing it, then I suggest to the hon. member that all he need do is to look at the speed with which the House of Commons has been dealing during the last week with the foreign investment review bill. The house has been dealing at the report stage with the government's proposal to deal with a matter that has been identified as one of too much American takeover of Canadian industry. The government has proposed legislation, the House of Commons has that legislation and for the last five days we have desperately been trying to break through the log jam of speeches that have come forward. It is not that the House of Commons is not seized of Canadian problems; it is that the House of Commons very often has not agreed upon a solution to those problems.
I did not criticize in general the opposition for taking the stand it has on the foreign investment review act. All I suggest is that it is their right, under the rules of the House of Commons, to delay that piece of legislation as long as they wish; but they cannot criticize the institution or the government for not providing solutions and criticize the government for not allowing it to come to a decision. It is the opposition that determines when a matter comes to a decision under the rules we now have in this House of Commons.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: Would the parliamentary secretary accept a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: Of course.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in response to the motion which I put forward the parliamentary secretary suggested that the House of Commons is doing the very work that a social council of Canada would do in my view, and therefore in his judgment it is not needed. Would he say that the work of the Economic Council of Canada is not needed because the House of Commons is doing its work, and therefore bodies such as that should be disbanded?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
If I may make my position clear, Mr. Speaker, I would disband almost all of these so-called institutions that surround us. I do not really believe that a proliferation of organizations of that nature, or a proliferation of government departments is getting us anywhere in dealing with the problems that face us today. It is my opinion
Broadcasting Act
that we should cut away the underbrush that surrounds so many of these organizations and institutions that grow up one with the other and do not contribute very much to the good of Canadian society.
This House of Commons has the responsibility for taking decisions on these items. We are here as freely elected representatives of the people, and we have the responsibility to bring attention to matters in a way which allows a decision to be taken. The problems and difficulties experienced by organizations like the Social Welfare Council, the Economic Council of Canada and the countless other councils that interpose themselves between the will of the House of Commons and the potential solution of problems make our position very difficult.
